items.title: Un ministre israélien appelle à faire en Cisjordanie «ce que nous avons fait à Gaza»
items.description: Le ministre israelien des Finances Bezalel Smotrich a appele dimanche 27 septembre l'armee a « entrer en guerre » en Cisjordanie occupee et a « y faire ce que nous avons fait a Gaza ». Interroge par Ynet sur les tensions securitaires, le chef du parti Sionisme religieux a aussi reclame le demantelement de l'Autorite palestinienne, qu'il qualifie d'« autorite terroriste ». La reference a Gaza donne a ces propos une portee particulierement lourde. Depuis octobre 2023, l'enclave palestinienne a connu des destructions massives et fait des dizaines de milliers de morts. Appeler a transposer cette methode a la Cisjordanie revient donc a envisager une extension considerable des operations militaires dans un territoire ou vivent trois millions de Palestiniens. Smotrich a parallelement plaide pour l'annexion de territoires a Gaza et dans le sud du Liban. Plus extreme que Bibi Ces declarations reprennent une ligne ancienne. Smotrich defend l'extension de la souverainete israelienne sur la Cisjordanie. En 2024, la Cour internationale de Justice a juge illicite la presence continue d'Israel dans le territoire palestinien occupe et demande l'arret de la colonisation. Israel conteste cette lecture et invoque ses imperatifs de securite. Sur le terrain, la situation s'est fortement deterioree. L'ONU a recense plus de 1 600 attaques de colons ayant fait des victimes ou cause des degâts entre janvier et août 2026, soit 6,7 attaques par jour. Des attaques palestiniennes contre des Israeliens ont aussi eu lieu. Dans ce contexte, les propos de Smotrich ne relevent pas seulement de la provocation : venant d'un ministre influent sur la politique israelienne en Cisjordanie, ils dessinent une orientation susceptible d'aggraver les violences et les deplacements. L'Autorite palestinienne a denonce un appel a la guerre et a l'annexion. a un mois des elections israeliennes , ces propos pesent aussi sur la campagne de Smotrich, figure de l'extreme droite.

items.title: Burkina: «Certains produits» pourraient être «exclusivement importés par l’Etat» contre la surenchère (Président)
items.description: Le président du Faso, le Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, répondant à la question sur la hausse des produits de grande consommation, a annoncé que, si les commerçants véreux persistent dans leur comportement répréhensible, «certains produits» pourraient être «exclusivement importés par l'Etat», lors d’un grand oral diffusé dans la nuit du dimanche 27 septembre à la télévision nationale. Lors de son face à face avec la presse, le chef de l’Etat burkinabè, le capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, s’est attardé sur la vie chère. Selon lui, la flambée des prix des produits de première nécessité s’explique par des phénomènes exogènes et endogènes. Malgré les efforts fournis par les structures de contrôle et de répression de l’Etat sur le territoire national, la situation persiste. «Il y a des prix qui peuvent flamber sans notre volonté. Sur le plan international, vous allez trouver certaines matières où le prix va flamber», a dit le capitaine Traoré, évoquant le cas du carburant dont le gasoil a subi une hausse de 75 F sur le litre. Selon lui, cette augmentation est à leur corps défendant, enchaînant que «le plus important, c'est à l'intérieur, c'est nous-mêmes». «Il y a des réactionnaires qui ont un agenda avec les impérialistes, qui font tout pour faire disparaître des produits pour faire la spéculation, qui sabotent, qui font monter les prix. Ils s'entendent et le font pour juste amener la population à rejeter la révolution. C'est leur seul objectif pour certains», a-t-il souligné. Le chef de l'Etat burkinabè, le capitaine Ibrahim Traoré Le chef de l’Etat a salué les structures de contrôle qui «font des efforts, ferment certaines boutiques». «C'est bien. Mais nous avons toujours dit aux commerçants véreux de faire attention et d'arrêter parce que l'Etat est en mesure de tout faire. Et s'ils n'arrêtent pas, le jour où l'Etat prend cette décision, ce sera irréversible». Il a insisté qu’après la création de Faso Yaar, si aujourd'hui les commerçants véreux persistent dans leur comportement, l’Etat va passer à une nouvelle dimension. «Et bientôt, certains produits, nous pourrons dire que ce sera exclusivement importé par l'État. Et là, Faso Yaar imposera le prix», a lancé le capitaine Ibrahim Traoré. Le président du Faso, le capitaine Ibrahim Traoré a ajouté que l’Etat «est en mesure de recruter des jeunes gens, les former, les installer et leurs donner le produit en avance avec le prix fixé partout sur le territoire, ils vont vendre. Et ceux (commerçants) qui sont dans ça (mauvais comportement), ils vont fermer boutique. Donc, on a dit aux gens de faire attention. Si on décide, on va le faire». Par Wakat Séra L’article Burkina: «Certains produits» pourraient être «exclusivement importés par l'Etat» contre la surenchère (Président) est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Lahore ATC extends physical remand of PTI's Hammad Azhar for 7 days in Jinnah House attack case
items.description: LAHORE: An anti-terrorism court (ATC) on Monday extended the physical remand of PTI leader Hammad Azhar for another seven days in the 2023 Jinnah House attack case . Sarwar Road police had booked several PTI leaders and workers on charges of attacking and vandalising the Jinnah House , which also serves as the residence of the corps commander, during the May 9, 2023 protests against the arrest of ex-premier Imran Khan. On Monday, police produced the former federal finance minister before ATC Judge Manzer Ali Gill upon the completion of his 21-day physical remand . During the hearing, a state prosecutor said police needed further remand to recover the suspect’s mobile phone and SIM, describing them as important pieces of evidence. He urged the court to extend the remand for a further seven days. Speaking before the court, Azhar questioned why further remand was being sought, saying he had already been kept on physical remand for 21 days in an alleged occurrence where he said he was not even present. “Even a murder suspect is sent on 14-day remand here. Has my offence become more serious than murder?” he asked. The former minister also complained that he had earlier not been allowed to meet his lawyers or family members — a concern also voiced earlier by his family before a court. The ATC then reserved its decision on the prosecution’s request for further remand, and later announced its decision, granting the police Azhar’s remand for another seven days. Meeting with family allowed, LHC told Separately, a two-member Lahore High Court (LHC) bench headed by Justice Syed Shahbaz Ali Rizvi disposed of a petition filed by Azhar’s mother and wife against the alleged denial of access to him during police custody. A Lahore ATC had already disposed of a similar plea filed by the family, directing them to approach the police on the matter. A Punjab government lawyer informed the LHC bench that Azhar had been allowed to meet his mother and wife. The law officer further said that the PTI leader would also meet his lawyer at the trial court on Monday. Relying on the government lawyer’s statement, the bench disposed of the petition. According to his family , Azhar was arrested on Sept 5. However, police said the next day they were unaware of his arrest, prompting the PTI leader’s mother to approach the LHC on Sept 7, and he was produced before an ATC the same day. Azhar, the son of late former Punjab governor Mian Muhammad Azhar , has been declared a proclaimed offender by multiple anti-terrorism courts for not joining the proceedings against him in cases related to the May 9 riots . Azhar had reappeared in public on May 22, 2024, a year after he had gone into hiding when the state launched a crackdown against the party leadership following the violent incidents of May 9 . At the time, the PTI leader had evaded arrest when the Counter-Terrorism Department raided the party’s secretariat in Islamabad.

items.description: Portée par la structure I Love Matam, l'initiative a réuni ce dimanche 27 septembre, à Matam des citoyens de cette commune autour du sport afin de collecter des fonds destinés à l'achat de fournitures scolaires pour des élèves issus de familles démunies. La commune de Matam a vibré au rythme d'une grande séance de fitness organisée par la structure I Love Matam. Au-delà de l'activité sportive, l'événement avait un objectif bien précis : lever des fonds grâce à la vente de t-shirts dont le prix unitaire est 50. 000 Gnf afin d'offrir des fournitures scolaires à des enfants dont les parents ne disposent pas des moyens nécessaires. Pour Ousmane Camara (OC), membre de la structure, cette initiative s'inscrit dans une vision plus large de développement communautaire. « Nous avons créé la structure I Love Matam pour rassembler les jeunes pour le développement de notre commune. Cette séance de fitness vise à collecter des fonds pour acheter des fournitures scolaires et les offrir aux élèves dont les parents n'ont pas les moyens », a-t-il expliqué. « Mettre cet espace au service de la jeunesse » Propriétaire du local ayant accueilli l'événement, l'honorable Lansana Diané s'est réjoui de voir revivre ce type d'activités dans une commune qu'il décrit comme un véritable creuset culturel. « Faire renaître un tel événement me donne un sentiment de joie et de fierté. Matam est une commune culturelle et sportive. Quand on dispose d'un tel espace, il faut le mettre à la disposition de la jeunesse et de la culture », a-t-il déclaré. Né et grandi à Matam, il affirme vouloir continuer à offrir ce lieu aux jeunes, considérant ce geste comme une manière de rendre à sa commune ce qu'elle lui a apporté. Un engagement fort pour l'éducation Présent à la rencontre, Kabinet Keïta, avocat général à la Cour d'appel de Conakry et citoyen de Matam, a salué la mobilisation des jeunes avant de prendre un engagement remarqué. « Je suis un produit de Matam à part entière. Je suis né à Matam, j’ai grandi à Matam. J'ai un devoir moral vis-à-vis de cette jeunesse de Matam. Je contribuerai, dans la limite de mes moyens, à aider les enfants de Matam à poursuivre leurs études », a-t-il déclaré. Il est allé plus loin en annonçant qu'il prendra en charge la scolarité d'un enfant de la commune. « Je prends l'engagement aujourd'hui de soutenir, jusqu'à la fin de son cursus scolaire, un enfant de Matam de votre choix. Je serai son parrain jusqu'à la fin de son cursus scolaire. » Le sport comme vecteur de santé et de citoyenneté Invité pour diriger la séance, Coach David a qualifié l'événement de première du genre. Selon lui, le sport dépasse largement le simple exercice physique. « Le sport, c'est la santé, la vie, la discipline et l'engagement. Il permet aussi de prévenir des maladies comme le diabète, l'hypertension ou les maladies cardiovasculaires », a-t-il souligné. Habitué à intervenir dans plusieurs communes de Conakry, le coach dit n'avoir jamais vu une telle mobilisation de jeunes autour d'une cause sociale. « C'est la première fois que je vois des jeunes d'une commune se mobiliser pour une même cause. C'est une preuve de citoyenneté, de solidarité et de bien-être. Si toutes les communes faisaient la même chose, le pays avancerait ». À travers cette première édition, I Love Matam entend démontrer que le sport peut devenir un puissant levier de cohésion sociale, tout en apportant un soutien concret à l'éducation des enfants les plus vulnérables de la commune. Sadjo Bah L’article Matam : une séance de fitness mobilise la jeunesse pour soutenir la rentrée scolaire est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Tunisie | Feuille de route de l’Ordre des ingénieurs pour la sécurité énergétique
items.description: Pour renforcer la sécurité énergétique en Tunisie et mettre fin aux problèmes survenus durant l’été 2026, avec les coupures intempestives d’électricité, l’Ordre des ingénieurs tunisiens a élaboré une «feuille de route énergétique», a indiqué le doyen des ingénieurs, Mohsen Gharsi, dans une publication sur le réseaux sociaux. Dans ladite feuille de route, l’Ordre des ingénieurs ne s’est pas limité à un simple diagnostic de la situation ou à des considérations générales sur le secteur, mais a mobilisé des compétences en ingénierie et des expertises pointues pour présenter des propositions pratiques dans le domaine de l’énergie. La problématique ne réside pas uniquement à augmenter la capacité électrique installée, mais dans la capacité réelle du système à répondre à la demande lors des pics de consommation, notamment en période de fortes chaleurs, a souligné Gharsi, en rappelant la nécessité d’une approche intégrée, englobant l’approvisionnement en gaz, la production électrique, la maintenance des réseaux, le développement des énergies renouvelables, le stockage de l'électricité, ainsi que la maîtrise de la demande, le financement des nouveaux projets et la gouvernance du système. La feuille de route propose plusieurs pistes opérationnelles, telles que le rétablissement de la capacité disponible grâce à des opérations de maintenance, la sécurisation de l’approvisionnement lors des pics de demande, le développement de l’autoproduction d’électricité à partir de l’énergie solaire, la protection des infrastructures critiques ainsi que le développement des systèmes de stockage. Le doyen des ingénieurs a également insisté sur la nécessité d’entamer dès maintenant les préparatifs pour l’été 2027, compte tenu du temps limité dont on dispose pour prendre des décisions et mener à bien les opérations de maintenance, la mobilisation des investissements et la mise en route des solutions envisagées. Il faut absolument éviter que ne se reproduisent, l’été prochain, les difficultés rencontrées par le pays durant l’été 2026, a-t-il insisté M. Gharsi a précisé que l’Ordre des ingénieurs ne cherche pas à se substituer à l’État, au gouvernement ou à la Société tunisienne de l’électricité et du gaz (Steg), mais qu’il met son expertise et ses compétences en ingénierie à la disposition de l’État afin de l’aider à relever les défis auxquels est confronté le secteur de l'énergie. L’objectif maintenant est de passer de la phase d’étude et de recherche des solutions à celle de la mise en œuvre des propositions et de la concrétisation des décisions, programmes et projets. Par ailleurs, M. Gharsi a salué les efforts des ingénieurs et experts ayant contribué à l’élaboration de cette feuille de route, affirmant que le rôle de l’ingénieur ne se limite pas au diagnostic des problèmes, mais englobe également la proposition de solutions et la participation à leur mise en œuvre. Il a conclu en affirmant la disposition de l’Ordre des ingénieurs à poursuivre le débat sur la feuille de route, à en enrichir les propositions et à contribuer à leur mise en œuvre, considérant que la sécurité énergétique ne relève plus de la seule dimension technique, mais qu’elle est également liée à la souveraineté économique, à la stabilité sociale et aux droits des générations futures. I. B. L’article Tunisie | Feuille de route de l’Ordre des ingénieurs pour la sécurité énergétique est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Supply Ministry postpones bread price review amid ongoing push from bakeries, mills
items.description: Supply Minister Sherif Farouk has asked for a week’s review period before the ministry responds to a request to raise its guideline consumer prices for two categories of non-subsidized bread, according to a source who was present at a Sunday meeting where representatives from bakeries and mills put forward their request. The request is their second in just a few months, following a dispute over the extent of the ministry’s role in setting and enforcing non-subsidized bread prices. Their push for higher guideline prices comes as the industry’s production costs rise steadily, with wheat prices spiralling again amid an escalation in the intensity of Russia’s war on Ukraine, and as domestic fuel prices continue to rise against the backdrop of the regional war. Farouk said the ministry would review price movements over the coming week, and, if prices did not fall over that period, the ministry would revise guideline prices for the tourist and fino bread categories, the source said. The ministry did not commit to a specific percentage increase. Senior representatives of the General Bakeries Division raised the issue of production costs at the meeting and called for a review of tourist and fino bread prices, proposing a 15 percent increase. Milling sector representatives also presented an update on the wheat and flour markets and recent pressures on production costs, particularly higher maritime shipping and logistics costs and rising global wheat prices amid the shipping disruptions in the Black Sea. Imported wheat reached record prices at the beginning of this week, rising to between LE16,600 and LE16,800 for Ukrainian wheat and LE17,000 for Russian wheat, compared with a maximum of LE12,200 to LE12,500 per ton in June. Bakeries selling tourist bread rely on the free market for their flour supplies, which account for more than 50 percent of production costs, the source said. Transport and other operating costs have also risen, leaving bakeries facing significant losses. The meeting is the latest in a series of calls bakeries have made to the ministry regarding tourist and fino bread prices, which intensified in August as flour and other production costs increased. The Supply Ministry did not respond to the demands, issuing a directive instead on August 4 to maintain the prices and weights for tourist and fino bread set in March . As bakeries continued to call for price increases, sources in the sector questioned the legal basis for the imposition of mandatory pricing on tourist bread, whose production inputs are not subsidized. Lawyer Khaled Ali previously told Mada Masr however that since wheat is a “strategic commodity,” the ministry has a role in market oversight. The ministry also threatened legal action against violators of its price directives at the time, with Interior Ministry statements later announcing “large scale campaigns to control supply crimes” against those violating Supply Ministry decisions on prices and weights. The changes in wheat and flour prices come amid volatility in global wheat markets, particularly continued tensions in the Black Sea region, the main source of Egypt’s wheat imports. Import data for the first eight months of the year showed that Russia and Ukraine together accounted for more than 82 percent of Egypt’s wheat imports, despite repeated announcements by the Supply Ministry of plans to diversify import origins. The post Supply Ministry postpones bread price review amid ongoing push from bakeries, mills first appeared on Mada Masr .

items.title: Structure des émissions du Sénégal sur le marché des titres publics : Les facteurs d’une amélioration
items.description: Le Sénégal a levé vendredi dernier 157 milliards FCfa sur le Marché des Titres publics. La particularité avec cette opération est un retour massif des investisseurs sur les Obligations de 3 et 5 ans. L’analyste financier Same Mbaye décrypte les facteurs « d’une sortie de crise ». Le 25 septembre 2026, l’État du Sénégal a sollicité le marché financier régional de l’Union monétaire Ouest-Africaine (Umoa) pour un montant de 150 milliards de FCfa, à travers une émission simultanée composée de Bons Assimilables du Trésor (Bat) à 364 jours et d’Obligations Assimilables du Trésor (Oat) à 3 et 5 ans. L’opération a suscité un montant total de soumissions de 157,89 milliards de FCfa, soit un taux de couverture de 105,26 %. Pour l’analyste financier et Trader, Same Mbaye, cette opération contraste nettement avec celle du 28 août 2026 (avant accord avec le Fmi), au cours de laquelle le Trésor avait mis en adjudication 70 milliards de FCfa. Les soumissions avaient, explique-t-il atteint un niveau supérieur au montant recherché, mais seulement 77 milliards de FCfa avaient finalement été retenus, soit un taux d’absorption de 67,65 %. Cette différence entre le volume des offres et celui des montants retenus traduit une sélection plus importante des propositions présentées par les investisseurs. Cependant, aux yeux de l’expert, l’analyse des rendements permet d’éclairer cette situation. Car le 28 août, les rendements moyens pondérés s’établissaient à 7,85 % pour le Bat, 7,77 % pour l’Oat à 3 ans et 8,24 % pour l’Oat à 5 ans. « Le Trésor pouvait ainsi privilégier les offres compatibles avec les conditions de financement recherchées et écarter certaines propositions comportant des exigences de rendement plus élevées. Il convient toutefois de présenter ce mécanisme comme une sélection des offres selon les conditions de prix et de rendement, plutôt que d’affirmer que toutes les offres rejetées étaient nécessairement « trop coûteuses » pour l’État », soutient Same Mbaye. Une situation qui se détend Poursuivant son analyse Same Mbaye estime que la situation s’améliore depuis l’adjudication du 11 septembre 2026. Pour un montant mis en adjudication de 100 milliards de FCfa, les soumissions atteignent 109,02 milliards, tandis que 101,34 milliards sont retenus, soit un taux de couverture de 109,02 % et un taux d’absorption de 92,96 %. Cette évolution, considère l’analyste financier, traduit une amélioration de l’adéquation entre les conditions proposées par le Trésor et les exigences des investisseurs, même si elle ne permet pas, à elle seule, d’établir une causalité précise. L’élément de contexte important qui intervient entre ces différentes adjudications selon lui est l’accord technique avec le Fmi. Le programme envisagé vise notamment à restaurer la stabilité macroéconomique et la viabilité de la dette, à réduire les vulnérabilités budgétaires et extérieures et à renforcer les finances publiques. « L’accord restait toutefois soumis à plusieurs conditions, notamment à l’approbation de la Direction et du Conseil d’administration du Fmi. Dans ce contexte, l’annonce du Fmi peut être considérée comme un facteur susceptible d’améliorer la visibilité des investisseurs sur le cadre de politique économique, mais il serait excessif d’attribuer directement l’amélioration des adjudications à cet événement », indique Same Mbaye. À l’en croire, la chronologie est compatible avec cette hypothèse, mais elle ne permet pas, à elle seule, d’établir une relation causale. D’autres facteurs peuvent également intervenir. Il s’agit notamment des anticipations de taux d’intérêt, des besoins de liquidité des investisseurs, des stratégies d’allocation des portefeuilles et des conditions générales du marché régional. Appétit pour le long terme Le 28 août 2026, rappelle Same Mbaye, les Oat à 3 et 5 ans représentaient déjà environ 68,3 % des montants retenus. Cette proportion atteint 75,5 % le 11 septembre 2026, puis 89,7 % le 25 septembre 2026. Il ne s’agit donc pas selon lui, d’un basculement brutal d’une préférence pour les Bar vers les Oat, mais plutôt d’un renforcement progressif de la demande et de l’allocation en faveur des maturités longues. « Le 25 septembre, sur les 157,89 milliards de FCfa de soumissions retenues, les Oat représentent près de 141,62 milliards FCfa, contre 16,27 milliards FCfa pour le Bat. L’Oat à 3 ans concentre à elle seule 96,74 milliards de FCfa, soit environ 61 % du montant total retenu », indique-t-il. Selon sa lecture, la dynamique est donc particulière car le taux de couverture diminue, passant de 162,60 % le 28 août à 105,26 % le 25 septembre, mais parallèlement le taux d’absorption augmente fortement, de 67,65 % à 100 %. « Cette combinaison est particulièrement intéressante. Elle signifie que, le 28 août, le Trésor avait reçu beaucoup d’offres mais n’en avait retenu qu’une partie, tandis que le 25 septembre, les montants proposés étaient plus proches du besoin de financement et ont été intégralement retenus », ajoute Same Mbaye. Il estime que les adjudications entre fin août et fin septembre 2026 suggèrent un renforcement de l’appétit des investisseurs pour les titres publics sénégalais, notamment les maturités longues. Cette évolution peut s’expliquer par les rendements proposés, les anticipations de taux et l’annonce du programme envisagé avec le Fmi. Toutefois, indique Same Mbaye, elle ne constitue pas à elle seule une preuve de confiance durable dans la trajectoire budgétaire. Pour lui, la consolidation budgétaire devra concilier soutenabilité de la dette, crédibilité financière, protection sociale et soutien à la croissance. Demba DIENG

items.title: One Reason People Are Spending So Much Time Alone
items.description: When showing up for others feels hard, some strugglers have lately steeled themselves with a version of this maxim: “Inconvenience is the cost of community.” It’s a reminder, oft-repeated on social media these days, that if you don’t want to be lonely—if you want to have robust relationships—you should occasionally do things that are effortful or even irritating, like cat sitting for a neighbor (or even just conversing with one!). You must give up on always pursuing maximum ease. The inverse of this adage is also true: Community is, all too often, the cost of convenience. In the journalist Gabe Bullard’s new book, Against Convenience , he argues that society’s relentless pursuit of faster and more frictionless experiences carries invisible costs, and he pushes back against how unthinkingly people often accept those costs as inevitable. Some of those costs are paid in dollars, as with monthly subscription fees to Netflix rather than the onetime cost of buying a DVD. Some are paid in lowered standards: more easily accessible entertainment that’s of poorer quality (YouTube shorts, anyone?), “smart” products that become obsolete faster than their analog forebears. But in reading the book, I noticed just how many of those costs are social. Take the portability of music, which started, long before smartphones or iPods, with the introduction of the Sony Walkman, in 1979—and the headphones that came with it (which have themselves become even more portable in the decades since). It is undeniably delightful to soundtrack your walks and bus rides with your favorite tunes, but, as Bullard writes, “isolation from others was a side effect (or a benefit, depending on your mood).” The convenience of the Walkman paved the way for a lifestyle in which Bullard can’t even hear his neighbors if they say hi, because the sound is now “among the noises canceled by my noise-canceling headphones.” Once you open your eyes to the tradeoff between convenience and community, you start seeing it everywhere. It’s more convenient to ride a Peloton bike at home alone than to go to a spin class full of other sweaty bodies (whom you might end up chatting with). Zoom meetings make working with distant colleagues much easier, but aren’t very socially nourishing. The gig economy is rife with this bargain. Ubers and Lyfts replace rides given by friends and trips taken on public transit. Delivery replaces meals out at local restaurants and time spent in stores of all kinds. [ Read: The one line Americans (weirdly) choose to wait in ] Sometimes, the reason an innovation is even considered convenient at all is because it allows you to do something in isolation. Such is the case with self-checkout. American shoppers love it—self-checkout lines frequently thread through a store even when staffed checkouts have little to no wait. But as Bullard points out, self-checkout is more work for customers, who have to do the cashier’s job themselves. And the machines are often less efficient than human cashiers, freaking out and freezing up because you jostled an item in the bagging area. “The only effort saved,” Bullard writes, “is whatever would have gone into engaging in basic niceties with a cashier.” Similarly, recognizing an opportunity in consumers’ desire to escape the alleged inconvenience of small talk, in 2019 Uber introduced a setting to request a “quiet ride”—for an extra fee, of course. Bullard is not the first to notice the isolating effect of many innovations, nor is it just modern conveniences that take us away from other people. Against Convenience references a famous Kurt Vonnegut anecdote in which the author ignores his wife’s advice to keep a box of envelopes at home and goes out shopping every time he needs a single one. On the way, he meets people, he enjoys the scenery of the neighborhood, and he has “one hell of a good time.” “We are dancing animals,” Vonnegut wrote. “How beautiful it is to get up and go out and do something.” But sacrifices are inevitable when we pursue convenience. Many of these exchanges are clearly worth it— I keep a box of envelopes at home—but Bullard convincingly argues that the costs of convenience, social and otherwise, have crossed a worrisome threshold in the 21st century. But what does it matter if you don’t want to talk with a cashier? If you’d rather stream a movie than sit in a room full of other people? You’re only avoiding strangers, after all. For one thing, talking with strangers brings a lot of benefits. Research has found that it’s mood boosting, and often more informative than people expect. One study, called “ Mistakenly Seeking Solitude ,” found that people regularly and incorrectly assume that being alone will make them feel better than interacting with another person. Avoiding these kinds of interactions is a detriment not only to yourself but also to the society you’re part of. It is often the so-called weak ties in someone’s network—the neighbor down the block you know only casually, the barista you order a latte from once a week—who are the most important in creating a rich sense of community. Because your networks overlap only a little, your weak ties can be a bridge to new connections, or they may know about job openings and social events that you and your close ties wouldn’t have come across on your own. Without weak ties, we wouldn’t have communities, just insular cliques. In some cases, choosing a seemingly innocent convenience for yourself can create inconvenience for others. Bullard gives the example of the Starbucks app—a “smooth and inviting” interface that lets you order your drink ahead of time, with whatever customizations you want, and simply walk into a store, pick it up, and leave. Undeniably convenient. But as a result, baristas’ jobs have gotten harder, due to the popularity of hypercustomized drinks that have gone viral on social media, facilitated by the ease of using the app. People would probably be less likely to order a sugar cookie iced matcha (Grande Iced Matcha Latte with oat milk, minus classic syrup, plus two pumps of sugar-cookie syrup, one pump of white mocha, vanilla-cream cold foam, and red and green sprinkles) if they had to say all of that to a person’s face and then actually watch them make it. And the proliferation of app orders means that the experience of walking into a Starbucks, and ordering and drinking your coffee there, is way more chaotic than it once was. The store is no longer a relaxing space in which to socialize, but rather “a place for fast, solitary transactions,” Bullard writes. A similar thing has happened at the many restaurants that have filled up with drivers waiting for delivery orders, crowding the diners who are there to share a meal in person. Individual conveniences add up to a deterioration of the public sphere. [ Read: Friendship, on demand ] And it isn’t just strangers whom people avoid. The preference for convenience over connection bleeds into our more intimate relationships too. Frictionless food deliveries and infinite online entertainment make it tempting to stay home alone rather than socialize—and many Americans are indeed becoming homebodies . People prefer to text, even though research shows that phone calls and in-person conversations make people feel more connected to one another. A main selling point of the AI companions that threaten to replace real ones is that they’re convenient. They’re always available, and always happy to talk about whatever you want, as long as you want, while real people have packed schedules and a desire for reciprocity. This is the environment in which “inconvenience is the cost of community” becomes a necessary reminder. Fittingly, if frustratingly, Against Convenience offers no convenient takeaway. That would be too easy! Bullard gestures at more collective, political solutions to some of the costs of convenience—unionization could create better conditions for workers caught up in the gig economy, legislation can address overuse of environment-destroying plastics (another of Bullard’s many examples of modern convenience). But ultimately, he writes, “every option has inescapable costs and change will take years.” Mostly, he recommends that individuals opt out of isolating temptations when they can for the sake of improving their quality of life. But he laments the limits of these personal decisions. “These individual actions bring individual comforts,” he writes. I think he’s being a little too pessimistic. Sure, one person canceling Amazon Prime may not register with Jeff Bezos. But when it comes to the social costs of convenience, individual actions can easily bring collective comforts. Taking out your headphones to say hello to a neighbor, scheduling dinner with friends instead of ordering delivery again—these choices pay immediate dividends in the form of connection, while also being a deposit in the shared, slower-yield investment account of building lasting community. items.title: How Biden Averted a War With Iran
items.description: S hortly after Hamas’s October 7 attack on Israel, President Biden asked me to help lead negotiations for a cease-fire and hostage-release deal. After some initial progress, the talks soon stalled, as fighting raged in Gaza. On February 21, 2024, I went to Cairo to restart them, carrying a new proposal. Egypt’s intelligence headquarters is in northern Cairo, surrounded by leafy avenues. Behind its gates is the heartbeat of the formidable Egyptian security state. Abbas Kamel, the head of the intelligence service from 2018 to 2024, was one of the country’s most powerful figures, although little known. A reserved man in his 60s, he had served in military intelligence with Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, now Egypt’s president, and the two had remained close ever since. Kamel was also central to the effort to stop the war in Gaza through a hostage deal. His intelligence service maintained direct channels to Hamas’s leaders in Gaza. Seated beside me in his office, Kamel lit his third cigarette and signaled to his aide Ahmed Abdel Khalek to bring the Israelis into the room. “Now!” Kamel said. Abdel Khalek skirted out the door, clutching an ever-present binder of papers. Kamel, slumped in his chair, seemed at the end of his patience. The task of delivering Hamas to a hostage deal was proving impossible. But cigarettes had a calming effect on him. The routine of sparking a lighter; the long inhale. He’d lean back, his eyes following a cloud of smoke wafting toward a fan on the ceiling. Then he’d sit up with the hint of a smile, or a new idea. Time to take up smoking , I thought. Only three months earlier, Kamel and I had sat in this same room and helped close the first cease-fire deal of the war. For seven days in November, the fighting stopped. More than 100 hostages were freed—women and children, including toddlers and grandmothers—in exchange for hundreds of Palestinian prisoners held by Israel. Humanitarian aid surged into Gaza and, with the guns silent, reached those in need across the Strip. The deal collapsed when Hamas, at the last moment, refused to release the younger women it was holding. Hamas proposed that we skip over them and begin discussing the older men, a clear violation of the deal that we had put together over weeks of negotiations. This article is adapted from Brett McGurk’s new book, Brink: Inside the Race to Free the October 7th Hostages . Israel refused. After midnight in Washington on December 1, 2023—early morning in Gaza—Hamas resumed firing rockets at Israel. Israel resumed air strikes. The war was back on. At the time, I had presumed that we’d succeed in putting together another deal, at least for the remaining women and the older men, including an American citizen. But Hamas held to maximalist demands. They included a return to the status quo of October 6, with the organization remaining in power in Gaza, reconstituted on the borders of Israel. After the massacres of October 7, when Hamas killed more than 1,000 and took more than 250 hostages, no Israeli leader would accept that outcome. [ Mark Bowden: The lesson of Israel’s success in the air ] Let alone Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s hard-line prime minister, who demanded as a war aim that Hamas be removed from power entirely. I would see him shortly after meeting Kamel. Our talks had further stalled as Iran ramped up attacks on Americans. In Iraq and Syria, U.S. troops came under near daily fire from Iranian-backed militias. Since October 7, these attacks had increased sevenfold from the year before, and the strikes aimed to kill. On Christmas Day, three Americans were wounded in a strike in northern Iraq, one grievously. Days later, the Iranian-backed proxy in Yemen, the Houthis, opened fire against ships in the Red Sea, including U.S. military vessels. The region was on the brink of a wider war. President Biden asked me to meet the Iranians in Oman, reactivating a back channel that had been used at times before the October 7 crisis. The day before my meeting, the Houthis launched their largest attack to date, firing about two dozen missiles and drones at U.S. and U.K. military ships. The back channel went nowhere. On January 28, 2024, two weeks after my meeting in Oman, an Iranian-supplied drone struck the living quarters of American troops in Jordan, killing three U.S. soldiers and wounding dozens. Biden finally chose to hit back, ordering the largest wave of air strikes across Iraq and Syria in more than a decade, including targeted strikes against the militia leader responsible for the attack in Jordan and the Iranian adviser in Baghdad enabling the militias. After that, the militias stood down. Now, finally, we were getting back to the hostage talks. Like Kamel, my patience was frayed. The war was now in its fifth month. Nearly 30,000 people had been reported killed in Gaza, including militants. More than 230 Israeli soldiers had died, and nearly 1,500 had been wounded. Hamas still held more than 100 hostages, including several American citizens. The carnage weighed on all of us. “We are mediators, Brett,” Kamel lamented. “It’s not my war, or your war; it’s their war, and they don’t want to stop. They both think they’ll win; there’s nothing to win.” He blew smoke to the ceiling. “They’ll destroy all of us, not just themselves.” The war could stop tomorrow with the release of six women hostages, I reminded him. These were the women passed over in the November deal, mostly civilians taken from a music festival. They’ll come last, he said. Hamas knew they were valuable to Israel. Kamel insisted that he was doing all he could, but we were stuck. Abdel Khalek returned with the Israeli delegation. Gaunt, with a military-style haircut graying like mine, Abdel Khalek was the Egyptian intelligence officer long charged with the Hamas file and was in direct contact with Yahya Sinwar, Hamas’s leader in Gaza and the mastermind of October 7. Few people outside Hamas knew the organization better. The Israeli delegation was led by Ronen Bar. With a shaved head and square jaw, Bar looked as if he’d stepped out of Fauda , the television drama about Shin Bet, the internal security agency he led. Bar was the main Israeli liaison with Hamas, and the Israeli official who most wanted a deal. He was willing to bend but not break Netanyahu’s guidance. To demonstrate his seriousness, Bar carried maps of Gaza rolled up in cases, and briefcases filled with the names of every Palestinian prisoner held by Israel, as well as all of the information Israel had on the hostages, their likely locations and conditions. Bar said Israel was prepared to finalize the details for an exchange of hostages for prisoners, down to the names of prisoners Hamas wanted released. He was also prepared to negotiate the conditions for a phased cease-fire, with Israeli forces withdrawing from Gaza to smaller perimeters as more hostages were freed by Hamas. If no hostages came out, Israeli forces would go in deeper. “That’s the formula,” Bar said. He challenged Kamel to convince Hamas to release at least one of the women. “I’m not Hamas!” Kamel said. Bar backtracked, meaning no offense. Rolling out a map in front of us, Bar explained that Israel was preparing a major military offensive in the southern Gaza city of Rafah. It would be the largest operation of the war so far. [ Arash Azizi: Iran is not ready for war with Israel ] Rafah was adjacent to Egypt’s border, and it was where Hamas remained militarily intact, still organized into brigades with subordinate battalions and smaller units beneath them. A network of tunnels deep underground fed into a main labyrinth to the north, known as the Kingdom, where Sinwar and his advisers had been hiding from Israeli forces, together with several hostages. Rafah was also where much of the civilian population had fled from Israel’s ongoing military operations elsewhere in Gaza. The only way to stop this planned operation, Bar said, was for Hamas to begin releasing hostages—starting with the women. Kamel said Hamas had opposite demands. Israel must withdraw completely from Gaza and guarantee a permanent cease-fire before it would release any hostages. Hamas and its leaders would remain in power, returning to the status quo of October 6. Meanwhile, Israel had to release all Palestinians held in Israeli prisons, regardless of crimes committed. That was Sinwar’s position, Kamel explained. “Impossible,” Bar said. He looked at me, wondering why I had recommended this meeting. “What is this?” he asked. In a negotiation with irreconcilable views, a mediator tries to create a “zone of possible agreement.” Between Hamas and Israel, there was none whatsoever. “Let’s consider a different approach,” I said. Together with Bill Burns, the CIA director and my partner in the hostage negotiations, I had developed a compromise framework to overcome the impasse. It would focus first on an area where both sides might agree: a cease-fire and the release of large numbers of Palestinian prisoners in exchange for a humanitarian category of hostages, starting with the remaining women and the older men, and then the sick or wounded. There were more than 30 hostages in those categories, including three Americans. The incentive for Hamas was a prolonged cease-fire—at least six weeks, longer than what was promised for the remaining women alone. And it could continue as long as talks continued for the remaining hostages, creating a chance to last a year or more. Bar said the Israeli side could accept that outline. Kamel smashed the butt of his cigarette in an ashtray. “They have greater demands,” he said. “You both know this. Sinwar won’t agree—” “Then push them! Push them!” Bar interrupted. “I do!” Kamel said. “What about you? Push Netanyahu!” I raised my arms to stop the two men from shouting at each other. Kamel retreated: “I trust you, Ronen. I trust you. But what does Netanyahu say?” Bar insisted that he was speaking for Netanyahu. “We need to hear it from your prime minister.” I was seeing Netanyahu the following day. “He’ll agree,” I predicted. “Release our girls, the war stops,” Bar insisted. We stood and shook hands. The three of us had no choice but to work together. Kamel asked Abdel Khalek to join us. “We’ll do our best,” Kamel said. Abdel Khalek shrugged, looking unconvinced. “Inshallah, inshallah,” he said. T he first thing a visitor to the prime minister’s office in Jerusalem sees is a wall draped with a map of Africa and the Middle East, with Israel, the size of a postage stamp, in the middle. Netanyahu greeted me in front of the map, then posed for a photo with a smile. Once the press had left the room, he offered his own bleak assessment of things across the map. Northern Israel had been evacuated. More than 80,000 people had relocated to escape daily rocket fire from Hezbollah in Lebanon. Southern Israel, the areas near Gaza, had also been evacuated, up to 50,000 people. Nearly 5 percent of Israeli territory was now a no-man’s-land. Netanyahu likened Hamas’s insistence on restoring its positions on Israel’s borders to national suicide. Israel won’t be a country, he said. People would never return to areas bordering Hamas or Hezbollah. His priority was creating the conditions for people to return home. In the south, that meant Hamas would never again exist adjacent to Israel. In the north, if a deal was reached in Gaza, he’d leave Hezbollah alone for now. If not, then Israel might have to clear Hezbollah from that border too. For more than 30 minutes, he never mentioned the hostages. “I’m here to discuss the hostage deal,” I reminded him. Netanyahu by this time was under criticism for not prioritizing the release of hostages over the military campaign inside Gaza. The criticism seemed valid. He was animated in discussing the military campaign, and far less so when discussing the hostages—when he chose to discuss them at all. He believed that it was only through a military campaign that Israel could secure the release of the hostages. There could not be one without the other. “So, how’s that all going?” Netanyahu asked me. “Not great, it seems.” I explained where we stood. The aim was to unite around the proposal we had discussed in Cairo, with Israel signed on and endorsed by Qatar and Egypt. “That places the onus squarely on Sinwar,” I said. “Why don’t you ask Hamas to accept something, then come to me,” Netanyahu said. This was not the way to negotiate with Hamas, he insisted. The group would pocket anything Israel accepted and then keep demanding more. “You’re doing things backward,” he said. [ David Frum: A test of strength ] Netanyahu also believed that time was on his side, not Sinwar’s. Israeli forces had finally discovered the Kingdom, thought to be the heart of Hamas’s extensive tunnel system. There, they had found millions of dollars in cash, along with Sinwar’s handwritten notes, laptops, and phones. Hamas’s leader had left the area before Israeli forces arrived, but they were now thought to be closing in. Eliminating Sinwar, combined with the looming Rafah operation, Netanyahu thought, would force Hamas to soften its demands and give up all the hostages, not just some. In the end, Netanyahu told me that he’d accept our proposal—a six-week cease-fire and a release of Palestinian prisoners in exchange for the women, elderly, and ill hostages—in principle. But the constant rounds of talks were grating on him, because they seemed to treat Hamas leaders as statesmen, as opposed to terrorists holding hostages in tunnels. “It won’t work,” he said. I agreed that eliminating Sinwar would be important and might help unlock a hostage deal, but until that happened, we should work to corner him—militarily and diplomatically. I called Abdel Khalek after the meeting. There was still no word from Hamas. I told him that Netanyahu accepted the proposal in principle. But even after spending nearly two hours with the prime minister, I could not be sure. Netanyahu was just impossible to pin down. Was he aiming to sabotage the talks, or was it his genuine view that Sinwar would only release the hostages with a knife to his throat? Until that proposition was tested, it was impossible to know. T wo weeks later , Hamas’s response to our proposal reinforced Netanyahu’s view that negotiations were going nowhere. The group rejected the compromise deal and stuck to its original demands. On March 18, Biden called Netanyahu and urged him to sweeten the deal by offering to release a larger number of Palestinian prisoners. Netanyahu reluctantly agreed, but Hamas would not budge. A week later, the United Nations Security Council voted on a resolution calling for an unconditional cease-fire in Gaza during the month of Ramadan, which was about to begin. The U.S. abstained from the vote, allowing the resolution to pass. Our UN team thought it would be too reputationally costly to veto it, as we had done with previous resolutions calling for an unconditional cease-fire—meaning without any hostages being freed. Ron Dermer, a member of Netanyahu’s cabinet who was formerly Israel’s ambassador to the U.S., called me after the vote. He said Hamas had praised the resolution and asked why our administration treated Israel as a “dishrag” at the UN. The charge was offensive, given Biden’s staunch support for Israel, and I told him as much, hanging up the phone. But while Dermer’s rhetoric was overheated, he was not wrong that Hamas saw the UN resolution as a strategic opening to strengthen its position. The day after the vote, Hamas’s leadership met with Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Khamenei, in Tehran, and pointed to Israel’s growing international isolation. The Houthis escalated their missile and drone attacks in the Red Sea. And with no progress in sight, Israeli negotiators withdrew from the talks altogether. “Israel will not surrender to Hamas’s delusional demands,” Netanyahu said in a statement. Our efforts to stop the war through a hostage deal were dead. Meanwhile, Biden was under political pressure at home—mainly from within his own party—to somehow force Israel to stop the war. Earlier in March, the journalist Jonathan Capehart had asked Biden whether Israel’s planned offensive in Rafah was a “red line,” given the potential impact on civilians. “It is a red line,” Biden said, adding that Israel “must pay more attention to the innocent lives being lost.” Biden later told us that he was referring to how Israel should conduct the operation, not whether it was conducted at all. In the same interview, he said he was “never going to leave Israel.” Around the same time, however, Vice President Harris told ABC News that Israel’s operation in Rafah would be a “huge mistake” and refused to rule out “consequences” if it went ahead. Looking back, it’s no wonder that Hamas never responded to our proposals during this period. We now know that in March 2024, as this political debate was taking place in the U.S., Sinwar was in a tunnel complex underneath Rafah. An avid consumer of news, he would have understood that relations between Biden and Netanyahu were approaching the boiling point. A year later, Ronen Bar visited Washington, D.C., and met with a group of former Biden aides. One of them asked plaintively what Biden should have done differently in the negotiations with Hamas. Bar pointed to this period in spring 2024, when Biden was said to be blocking Israel’s operation in Rafah. From Bar’s vantage point, that perception had hardened Hamas’s position, making it more difficult to free the hostages and end the war. “That was your biggest mistake,” he said. O n the morning of April 1 , a group of Israeli officials crowded into the White House Situation Room to lay out their humanitarian plans for the Rafah operation. Following Biden’s comments, we had made clear that the operation should not begin before civilians had the opportunity to leave the area. Before the meeting started, Israel’s ambassador, Michael Herzog, and its military attaché, Major General Hidai Zilberman, asked to speak with me outside the room, so as not to be overheard. Zilberman said that Israel was about to conduct an air strike in Damascus. The target was Mohammad Reza Zahedi, a senior Iranian officer responsible for proxy operations across Syria and Lebanon, including Hezbollah. That was not particularly surprising. Zahedi was a legitimate target for the Israelis, given the ongoing Hezbollah attacks in northern Israel. I thanked Zilberman for informing me. [ The Editors: The Biden doctrine ] “One more thing,” he said. He was a giant man with a shaved head, resembling a heavyweight boxer, and his large dome leaned toward mine. Iran might claim that the building about to be attacked was a consulate, Zilberman said, but it was not. I pressed him: Diplomatic facilities are protected under international law. If the target in Damascus was a consulate, it was off-limits. Zilberman insisted that the Israelis had seen no evidence that was the case. By the time we got out of the meeting, the building had been flattened and Zahedi and several of his associates were dead. Iran declared that it viewed the strike as an attack on Iranian territory and vowed to strike Israel in retaliation. We soon picked up reports that Iran was preparing for a missile attack against Israeli cities. It was hard to believe at first. For decades, Iran had fought using proxies, allowing itself some deniability and reducing the risk of retaliatory attacks inside its own borders. But more reports came in showing preparations for a massive strike—a combination of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and drones aimed at hundreds of targets across Israel. In urgent consultations with the Israelis, we calculated how many defensive missile interceptors would be needed in a worst-case scenario. Israel has some of the world’s most sophisticated air defenses, including Arrow systems that target missiles at the edge of outer space and closer-range defenses that take out lesser threats. But based on what we were seeing from Iran, even that capability might not be enough. Zilberman visited my office with a formal request for U.S. military forces to help defend Israeli territory—air wings, destroyers, and missile defenses. The request was extraordinary, and it broke with Israel’s traditional doctrine: We defend ourselves, by ourselves. When I told Biden’s chief of staff, Jeff Zients, and other top White House aides that we might be about to see the largest ballistic-missile attack in history, with Israel as the target, they were visibly alarmed—both for the people who lived there and for how it might affect the 2024 election. The focus in the West Wing had shifted to the campaign, and Biden’s team wanted him to appear strong and in command, not captive to events. Biden was determined to defend Israel, but his frustration with the crisis—and with Netanyahu—was growing. The president was known for picking up the phone at all hours—he once called my mother out of the blue. But in the first quarter of 2024, he spoke with Netanyahu only a handful of times, compared with nearly 20 calls in the last quarter of 2023. Relations between the two leaders deteriorated further after Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer called for Israel to hold elections and replace Netanyahu. Netanyahu believed that Biden had put Schumer up to it; Biden denied this, but later called Schumer’s remarks a “good speech.” Late in the day on April 1, hours after Israel’s attack in Damascus, an Israeli drone struck a convoy in northern Gaza and killed seven aid workers affiliated with World Central Kitchen, a nonprofit led by the chef José Andrés. The Israelis had welcomed Andrés and his organization into Gaza, viewing them as more trustworthy than the U.N. The strike was a tragedy—Israel called it a “grave mistake”—and it fueled calls for an immediate and unconditional cease-fire. Biden was now being criticized from all sides: The left saw him as too weak to rein in Israel, while the right saw him as too weak to force Hamas to free the hostages and, more broadly, as having no articulable plan to end the war. Against this backdrop, Biden and Netanyahu spoke on April 4. The all-out Middle East war that the U.S. had sought to avoid was fast approaching. Iran had hundreds of ballistic missiles and drones aimed at Israel. Israel was planning a counterattack. The hostage talks with Hamas were dead. The humanitarian crisis in Gaza was worsening. When I walked into the Oval Office that day, Biden’s face was red like a beet. I sat in front of his desk with a larger crowd than usual, including Zients, Secretary of State Antony Blinken, and Burns. Everyone sensed that something was about to give. “What the fuck am I telling this guy?” Biden asked. There were different views. Some people advised the president to simply tell Netanyahu that the war was over; if he refused, we’d cut Israel’s support. Biden was hearing this sentiment on the campaign trail from parts of the Democratic Party. But he asked what would happen if we cut military assistance while hostages remained in tunnels and the war continued, with Israel under attack from multiple directions. “We’re on the side of Iran?” he asked rhetorically. Burns advised that a hostage deal remained the only path to a cease-fire. That meant maintaining support for Israel while trying to restart the negotiations with Hamas and easing the immense human suffering in Gaza as much as possible. I agreed with Burns but chose not to say much, taking in the scene and trying to read Biden, who seemed ready to blow his stack. Jake Sullivan, the national security adviser, discussed Israel’s preparations for the missile attack and its request for U.S. military support. On Biden’s desk were orders, recommended by Secretary of Defense Lloyd Austin, for the emergency deployment of additional forces to the region. Biden said he approved them, without hesitation. He then asked how we might return to the hostage deal. It seemed hopeless, but Burns suggested that there might be an opportunity to use Iran’s attack to our advantage. If we helped defeat it, Netanyahu would owe us, and Sinwar would see that even a direct attack by Iran could not improve Hamas’s position. “If we don’t defeat it?” Biden asked, unconvinced. The answer was regional war. Israel had already prepared a counterattack in the event that Iran’s missiles caused Israeli casualties. “Great,” Biden said. The Situation Room connected the call. Biden jumped in. “Bibi, man, what the fuck are you doing?” He gripped the phone tight. “You think I’m Santa Claus? No Santa in Israel, pal.” When Netanyahu asked what he meant, Biden said he could cut off military aid to Israel with the snap of a finger, leaving the country on its own. Netanyahu retorted that Israel would defend itself even without the United States. (We later learned that he concluded from this call that we were cutting military supplies.) [ Franklin Foer: How Netanyahu lost America ] Returning to his prepared points, Biden made specific requests regarding humanitarian aid and opening additional crossings into northern Gaza. Netanyahu began to discuss Israel’s preliminary assessment of the strike on the aid workers, claiming that it was more complicated than what was being reported in the news—a tragic miscommunication. Biden interrupted: “I don’t want to hear it, Bibi.” He said he’d help defend Israel against Iran, but then the U.S. would move immediately to end the war and free the hostages. “That’s the deal, pal.” He hung up abruptly. It was a short call. If not for the pending Iranian attack, the U.S. might have taken irreversible measures against Israel at this juncture. My own mind wrestled with whether this might have been a better course. We all wanted the war to end. It was a sickening horror in every dimension. Was the means to that end the hostage and cease-fire deal—the course we had been on—or simply telling Israel to stop, even as it was under attack on multiple fronts? If there was a better way to end the crisis, Biden would have taken it. He had tried a UN resolution calling for an unconditional cease-fire. He had tried increasing public pressure. Those steps only seemed to make the situation worse. There were multiple belligerents in this conflict. Increasing public pressure on Israel did not stop the war. It seemed to encourage those fighting against it. I had never seen Biden so frustrated—spitting mad, literally. Sullivan took out a note card to draft the readout, the official summary of the call. We debated whether to publicly threaten to cut military aid to Israel. Biden was not comfortable doing so at a moment when hundreds of Iranian missiles were being readied for launch. The final readout warned that U.S. policy “will be determined by our assessment of Israel’s immediate action” on “specific, concrete, and measurable steps to address civilian harm, humanitarian suffering, and the safety of aid workers.” At the same time, it said that Biden had “made clear that the United States strongly supports Israel in the face of [Iran’s] threats.” This was the paradox. For all Biden’s frustration with the situation, and with Netanyahu, Israel was under attack from common enemies. Fueling Iran’s confidence was the belief that Biden was under pressure to break with Israel. Iran seemed to believe that a missile attack against Israel might help push Biden over the edge. That proved to be a miscalculation. O n Saturday, April 13 , Biden took his seat at the head of the table in the Situation Room. He’d just come from his home in Rehoboth Beach, Delaware, and had two shirt buttons undone beneath his jacket. I had been at the White House since early in the morning to help coordinate Israel’s defense with other countries in the region. Iran’s attack began around 3:30 p.m. with 200 drones, followed 90 minutes later by 30 cruise missiles. Those were all in the air and flying toward Israel by the time Biden arrived. The ballistic missiles had yet to launch. The flight time for drones from Iran to Israel was three hours. Cruise missiles took about half that time, and ballistic missiles took 13 minutes. Iran’s launch sequence ensured that all of the attacks would converge on Israel at the same moment. The aim was to overwhelm Israeli air defenses and allow the heavy-payload ballistic missiles to hit their targets. Earlier that day, Tehran had sent a message warning that if the U.S. helped defend Israel, it could no longer restrain militias in Iraq and Syria, which had not fired a shot against U.S. personnel since our air strikes in February. Meanwhile, Herzog and Zilberman had visited my office to review Israel’s potential response to an Iranian attack. If Iran’s missiles killed Israelis, Zilberman said, then Iran had no idea what was coming. His large fist pounded my desk. Seated in the Situation Room with Biden were Austin, Blinken, Sullivan, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs General C. Q. Brown, and other senior advisers. Harris was on a video feed from Los Angeles. General Erik Kurilla, overseeing U.S. operations, was on video from his headquarters in Tampa, Florida. Biden asked about our preparations. Over the previous 96 hours, the U.S. had strengthened defenses in and around Israel, deployed military assets and fighter squadrons, and coordinated with a makeshift coalition of Arab and European states. “Good as we could do,” Austin said. “Where’s Bibi?” Biden asked. Netanyahu was in an underground command center in Israel, where he planned to ride out the attack and then determine how to respond. Burns sketched out possible scenarios. If Iran’s attacks killed Israelis, Israel would launch a large air attack on Iran. This would bring a state-on-state conflict to the Middle East for the first time in decades, with the risk of drawing in the U.S. Biden said he would not allow that to happen. We may not have a choice , I thought. Kurilla reported that American air squadrons were taking down dozens of slow-flying Iranian drones over Syria, Iraq, and Saudi Arabia. He called it a turkey shoot. One of those pilots was Lieutenant Colonel Kevin Murphy. Days earlier, he had been at home in North Carolina, he later recalled in Air & Space Forces Magazine . He arrived in the Middle East less than 24 hours before it became the largest aerial combat zone since the Korean War. Murphy and his weapons officer, Major George Welton, along with the rest of their squadron, shot down two dozen drones. Defeating these first salvos was critical for saving the main air defenses for the ballistic-missile attack. “Ballistic missiles could be the challenge,” Austin said. Iran’s ballistic missiles could descend at speeds of 5,000 miles per hour, striking targets with precision while carrying a 1,000-pound warhead. U.S. and Israeli air-defense systems are the best in the world, but if Iran launched enough missiles, it was a near certainty that some would get through and reach their targets. In the eastern Mediterranean, American destroyers readied in coordination with Israeli land-based defenses. Patriot anti-missile batteries operated by the U.S. Army stood by across the Middle East, from Iraq to Jordan, scanning the skies for targets. “What’s your worst case?” Biden asked. Nobody knew for sure how many missiles the Iranians might shoot at once. The worst-case scenario was thought to be 50 or more. “So we just wait?” Biden asked. Heads nodded. The screen on the wall in front of me suddenly showed yellow streaks rising from Iran. Kurilla opened his mic: “Mr. President, Mr. Secretary, we have confirmed ballistic-missile launches. Thirty launches total from tracks.” “We can handle 30,” Austin said. The streaks rose from across Iran and built up speed as they approached the edge of the atmosphere. Kurilla, moments later: “Thirty new launches, Mr. President.” “Thirty new launches?” Biden asked. Kurilla confirmed that there were now 60 missiles in the air. More yellow streaks rose from Iran as the first wave curved horizontally across Iraq, heading for targets in Israel. “That’s a challenge,” Austin said. “Six minutes before defenses engage,” Kurilla said. I had never felt so helpless in this room, the command center of the most powerful country on Earth. I knew what interceptors we would fire first, the backups if they failed—everything that was about to transpire. Yet, for the first time ever while seated at that table, I bowed my head and prayed. More yellow lines rose from the digital map of Iran. Kurilla confirmed a third salvo. Ninety missiles were now in the air, coming in three waves. “I’m dropping to coordinate defense,” he said. “Ninety?” Biden said. Moments later, more streaks. I couldn’t believe my eyes. Kurilla confirmed a fourth salvo. There were now more than 100 ballistic missiles flying toward Israel. Nobody said a word. Many, like me, were seemingly in quiet prayer. [ Andrew Exum: Netanyahu doesn’t care about his friendship with Biden ] Four minutes before the missiles reached the range of our defenses, the room was so quiet that you could hear a digital red clock humming on the wall. Then streaks appeared from the other side of the screen: interceptors launching from Israel and our destroyers at sea, and Patriots from elsewhere. Israel’s Arrows built speed to Mach 9, more than one mile per second. American destroyers fired SM-3 interceptors that traveled even faster, reaching incoming missiles above the atmosphere in tens of seconds. Screens across three walls tracked hundreds of converging missiles and interceptors, like a multiplayer video game. It did not seem real. Suddenly, bright-white flashes burst onto the screens: Satellite imaging was picking up the interceptors as they exploded 60 miles above the Earth. “Defenses engaged,” Kurilla said, stating the obvious. The entire Middle East, from Israel to Lebanon, Syria, and Jordan, was covered in apocalyptic white airbursts. Through his cockpit window 6,000 miles from the White House, Murphy saw interceptors launch to engage missiles far above him. There were massive explosions in all directions, then wreckage descending around his aircraft. “You fly through it,” he recalled. “You think skinny, you pray, and you continue on the heading that you’re on.” “Impacts?” Biden asked. Reports incoming, Kurilla said. “We won’t know straightaway,” Brown added. The door opened. A watch officer delivered a note from Nate Swanson, my lead adviser on Iran. It was a message from the Iranians, saying that what was in the air now was the end of the attack, but that they would launch a larger salvo if Israel responded. I read the note to Biden. He nodded, too much information coming in at once. The screens gradually cleared. All of the missiles had either reached their targets or been intercepted. There was nothing to indicate what had happened at ground level. “Erik, report,” Austin said. Kurilla answered that we had no confirmed impacts in Israel. The defenses appeared to have been successful. Many in the Situation Room leaned back in their chairs with sighs of relief. “Thank God,” someone said. I remained on edge. “We won’t know for certain yet,” Austin warned. Kurilla again: “Israelis confirm no significant impacts.” “Pretty good,” Austin said quietly. “Unless Iran fires more.” “They claim they won’t,” I said. Biden nodded to Sullivan. “Get Bibi on the line.” “What do you want to say to him?” I asked. “I just saved his ass, that’s what. Cut this off here.” “Take the win,” Sullivan added. Outside the room, I connected with the Israelis in their bunker. Netanyahu asked for 30 minutes before taking the call, which further riled up Biden. “Does he know we just saved his ass?” Biden asked. This was the first time the U.S. military—let alone the U.S. military together with a coalition of European and Arab countries—had fought to defend Israel. The moment was not lost on Biden. Now the question was how to leverage it. Sullivan recommended that we use the time to craft what Biden would say to Netanyahu. “Go,” the president said. “Hurry up.” Deputy National Security Adviser Jon Finer and I went with Sullivan to his office and huddled behind his desk as he typed out talking points. For the key takeaway, we chose to use Sullivan’s formulation (“Take the win”) instead of Biden’s (“I just saved your ass”). We recommended that the president ask Israel to respond in a way that inflicted few casualties and aimed to end the direct exchange of fire. Then we would get back to the hostage deal. Netanyahu was ready for the call. Back in the Situation Room, we handed Biden a draft. He read it aloud, made a few adjustments, and said, “Put him on.” Netanyahu’s voice came through the speakers: “Hi, Joe, quite a night here.” “Looks like you’ve come out okay, Bibi.” By this time, only one casualty had been confirmed, a young girl wounded by falling shrapnel in southern Israel. “I’m still getting reports, but yes, the good news is the defenses worked.” “ Our defenses, Bibi—” “Joe, we worked together, our militaries and our teams. It’s historic. Unbelievable, a coalition of militaries; I know it. But, Joe, the lesson is that these maniacs are willing to fire hundreds of missiles at Israel–this has never been done before, nowhere.” The lesson was that Israel needed the United States, Biden pressed. “Against these maniacs from Iran; they’re your enemies too,” Netanyahu said. “Take the win,” Biden said abruptly. He explained that Israel had every right to respond, but the response should be developed with us and designed to deter, not escalate. Take your time and get it right, he urged. Netanyahu was noncommittal. He had to see what the light of day brought to Israel. “We need to teach these maniacs a lesson,” he said. Biden again pressed Bibi to take the win and work with us on a response. He said our military team would coordinate with Netanyahu’s. “Let’s have our teams discuss it,” Netanyahu said. They agreed to talk again soon. The call dropped. Biden turned back to us with his palms up, asking for our views. “He heard you,” Sullivan said. Austin said he’d work with the Israelis on response options. It was approaching 10 p.m., with a long night ahead. We soon received another message from Iran, warning us again not to support Israel. Then a public message from Iran’s UN mission in New York: “US MUST STAY AWAY!!” For the first time since October 7, I thought, Tehran seemed anxious. The following morning, Biden spoke with the pilots and air commanders responsible for the defense, including Murphy and Welton’s squadron. He expressed gratitude as commander in chief for what they had just done. “It’s what we train for, sir,” said one of the pilots. “I don’t think you ever trained for last night,” Biden said. “There’s never been anything like it. The only reason we’re not in a major war right now is because of what you did. I mean it, guys. Thank you, thank you, thank you. You saved the world; I mean it. God bless you.” This article is adapted from Brett McGurk’s new book, Brink: Inside the Race to Free the October 7th Hostages .

items.title: Irish players refuse handshakes, wear black armbands in Nation Leagues clash against Israel
items.description: Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in a Nations League clash on Sunday amid an eerie and sombre atmosphere that saw the Irish players wear black armbands over the war in Gaza. Ireland’s players also bowed their heads as the Israeli national anthem was played at the near-empty Debrecen stadium in Hungary. The teams skipped the traditional pre-match handshakes and did not exchange pennants either. Troy Parrott made a heart sign with his hands after opening the scoring on 14 minutes, while Jack Moylan kissed the Irish badge on his jersey and his black armband after netting the third goal 25 minutes in. Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson said his team had “raised awareness worldwide” about the Gaza conflict after they chose not to shake hands with Israeli players. The game, in which Israel were the nominal hosts, had been in doubt earlier in the week until Ireland’s players voted overwhelmingly to fulfil the fixture, despite pressure from back home to boycott the match. Only one player, goalkeeper Gavin Buzunu, pulled out, saying “it would be wrong to participate” in either this match or the return fixture in Serbia on October 4 due to the “killing of innocent people”. “It has been so difficult for so many players,” Icelander Hallgrimsson told broadcaster RTE after the game. “I hope that will not be in the next game because they have shown support to the protest, they have raised awareness worldwide, not only in Ireland, on the subject and that is normally the reason for protesting, to raise awareness of a situation. “I think these players have done that with all their actions, with all that they have been saying. No more than Gavin Bazunu, but the others have done it here on the pitch and how they have shown their actions, so I hope people understand that.” Since Ireland were drawn in the same Nations League group as Israel in February, prominent Irish figures including sportspeople, fan groups and pro-Palestinian campaigners have protested against the matches going ahead. The Irish federation did not reserve any tickets for fans to attend the match and public broadcaster RTE was due to show it without commentary. Israeli minister irked Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar accused Ireland of being “on the wrong side of history” over the players’ actions. In a lengthy post on X, Saar referenced the Irish team of 1939 giving the Nazi salute ahead of a match against Germany in Bremen. He also referred to Irish neutrality during the Second World War and the condolences offered by then-prime minister Eaemon de Valera to the German representative in Dublin following Adolf Hitler’s death. “Almost 90 years have passed. Ireland’s unique talent for finding itself on the wrong side of history remains intact,” he added. “Sports, soccer, basketball, everything is for the public, the people, and not for politics,” 31-year-old software development teacher Mol Michael, draped in an Israeli scarf, told AFP . “Once you decide, because of politics, to cancel the Irish audience, this is a really stupid move from Ireland, in my opinion.” Ireland has long been a strong supporter of the Palestinian cause, with sympathy often linked to the country’s own history of British rule. Dublin formally recognised a Palestinian state in 2024 alongside Spain and Norway, and has repeatedly criticised Israel over its relentless bombardment of Gaza.
